query: For titanium alloys used as structural materials, formulate one hypothesis for an intervention that could increase surface hardness and wear resistance. Specify the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to the untreated alloy, the service or test conditions under which the effect should hold, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a controlled experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Plasma nitriding Ti–6Al–4V alloy using an NH3–N2 gas mixture at 750 °C for 4 hours increases surface hardness and wear resistance by forming a hardened Ti–N compound layer at the alloy surface, a process mediated by nitrogen diffusion and the development of compressive residual stresses.
generation.material_initial_state: Ti–6Al–4V alloy in its standard annealed or Widmanstätten microstructural state with baseline surface hardness and wear resistance.
generation.intervention: Expose the Ti–6Al–4V specimens to a plasma nitriding process at 750 °C for 4 hours in an atmosphere composed of NH3 and N2 in a 1:2 ratio.
generation.conditions: The enhanced properties are expected to hold under ambient laboratory conditions during standardized dry sliding wear tests (for example, pin‐on‐disk tests performed at moderate loads) and under comparable low-cycle fatigue tests where the surface state is critical. The temperature, gas composition, and treatment duration are tightly controlled as specified in the cited reports.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a surface compound layer consisting of titanium nitrides (primarily δ–TiN and ε–Ti2N) along with an underlying nitrogen diffusion zone.
generation.mechanism: Nitrogen diffuses into the Ti–6Al–4V matrix during plasma nitriding, leading to the in situ formation of hard Ti–N phases. These phases obstruct dislocation movements and create compressive residual stresses, which together raise the surface hardness and provide a barrier against wear by reducing friction and material removal.
generation.predicted_outcome: The nitrided specimens should exhibit a significant increase in microhardness (potentially in the range of three- to fourfold improvement relative to the untreated alloy) and show a marked reduction in wear volume during standardized wear tests.
generation.baseline: Untreated Ti–6Al–4V alloy, which has lower microhardness and greater wear rate under identical test conditions.
generation.boundary: While the formation of hard nitrides improves wear resistance and hardness, excessively high nitriding temperatures or durations might lead to increased surface roughness or brittleness. The positive effects are expected under controlled process parameters, and the benefits may be reduced under fatigue conditions where roughness plays a counteracting role.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements in hardness and wear resistance may depend on minor variations in process control, and the interplay between enhanced hardness and increased surface roughness introduces some uncertainty regarding the overall tribological performance under cyclic loading.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Ti–6Al–4V alloy samples: one set remains untreated (control) and the other is plasma nitrided under the specified conditions. After processing, measure surface microhardness using Vickers hardness testing and perform standardized pin‐on‐disk wear tests under identical loads and sliding conditions.
measurements: Vickers microhardness values at the surface and across the nitride layer
Wear volume or wear rate from the pin‐on‐disk tests
Surface morphology assessments (e.g., via SEM) to confirm the formation of Ti–N phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nitrided samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase (e.g., less than a 20% improvement) in microhardness and a corresponding reduction in wear volume compared to the control group, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The growth of the Ti-N compound layer was enhanced by the use of an NH3-N2 mixture during the plasma nitriding of the Ti6Al4V alloy. After nitriding at 750 °C for 4 h in an NH3-N2 (1:2) atmosphere, a Ti-N compound layer approximately 2 μm thick was formed on the Ti6Al4V alloy. The Ti-N compound layers are typically much harder than the titanium alloy substrate. In comparison to the un-nitrided titanium alloy, samples nitrided in an NH3-N2 mixture exhibited the complete elimination of stick–tear and plowing wear throughout the duration of the test, resulting in undetectable wear loss when in contact with bearing steel. The oxide layer formed on the wear track by the transfer of material from the counterpart steel ball reduced the average friction coefficient from approximately 0.55 to 0.30 under an 8N load. The formation of the Ti-N layer not only enhances the hardness and wear resistance of the titanium alloy but also increases its corrosion resistance.

By varying the microstructure and nitriding parameters, the fatigue strength of a material can be affected. Tokaji et al. [] reported that the fatigue strength of pure titanium was increased by nitriding, while it was decreased in the case of Ti-6Al-4V. Based on detailed observations of fatigue crack initiation, growth, and fracture surfaces, the improvement and the reduction in fatigue strength by nitriding of pure titanium and Ti-6Al-4V alloys were primarily attributed to enhanced crack initiation resistance and to premature crack initiation of the nitride layer, respectively. However, Farokhzadeh et al. [] achieved an improvement on the fatigue proprieties of the Ti-6Al-4V alloy plasma nitrided at a low temperature (600 °C). These results were different than those obtained by an elevated temperature treatment (900 °C) as well as conventional gas/plasma nitriding treatments reported in the literature [,,]. The thin morphology of the compound layer restricted the extent of premature crack initiation from the surface. Increased fatigue life of the plasma nitrided specimens in tests at higher stresses can be attributed to compressive residual stress in the nitride layers and in the nitrogen diffusion zone, thereby inhibiting crack nucleation at the alloy surface. This is in agreement with another study by Rodriguez et al. []. According to Farokhzadeh et al. [], the nitride layer reduces the extent of brittle failure on the specimen surface while the diffusion zone provides mechanical support. As per the study of Morita et al [], the formation of these layers after plasma nitriding increases the surface hardness of the alloy, which in turn increases the resistance to movement of dislocations and, as a consequence, increases the fatigue strength of the alloy. Rocha [], reported that delay in crack nucleation in plasma nitrided specimens is due to the difference in the Young modulus between the titanium alloy matrix (100 GPa) and the titanium nitrides formed on the plasma nitride surface (400 GPa). When high stresses are applied to the fragile nitride layer, it causes the nucleation and the growth of a crack in this layer.
